note: Bart 11-11: Babylon worlds, Nebuchadnezzar II. Sources: Koldewey excavations; Ishtar Gate and Processional Way (Pergamon Museum, Berlin); Etemenanki.

sheets.subject: Babylon c. 575 BCE (after Koldewey's excavations): the Ishtar Gate seen from the front down the Processional Way: a tall double gate with crenellated towers either side of a high arched passage, entirely faced with deep blue glazed bricks, rows of yellow and white relief bulls (aurochs) and dragons (mushhushshu) in horizontal registers; the city wall running off to both sides.

Babylon c. 575 BCE (after Koldewey's excavations): (1) the wall of the Processional Way, 12 m high: deep blue glazed brick with a row of striding yellow-maned lions in relief between bands of white and yellow rosettes, crenellations on top; (2) a plain baked-brick kerb, 0.6 m high.
The Processional Way of Babylon: large pale limestone paving slabs set in rows along the road, a central strip of slabs edged with reddish breccia, worn smooth
The Processional Way of Babylon: large pale limestone paving slabs set in rows along the road, a central strip of slabs edged with reddish breccia, worn smooth

Babylon c. 575 BCE (after Koldewey's excavations): the great ziggurat Etemenanki seen across the sacred precinct: a huge square stepped tower of several receding stages of baked brick, a wide triple staircase climbing the front to the second stage, a small blue-glazed temple on the summit; in front of it the long buttressed enclosure wall of the precinct with towered gates.

Babylon c. 575 BCE (after Koldewey's excavations): (1) the enclosure wall of the sacred precinct, 9 m high, baked brick with tall shallow buttresses and a toothed crenellated top; (2) a low platform of baked brick, 1 m high, with a few steps.
The wide court of the temple precinct of Babylon: baked bricks laid in bitumen in large even rows, dusty and worn
The wide court of the temple precinct of Babylon: baked bricks laid in bitumen in large even rows, dusty and worn

Babylon c. 575 BCE (after Koldewey's excavations): the Euphrates flowing through Babylon: the far bank lined by a massive quay wall of baked brick set in bitumen, the city wall above it with regular square towers and crenellations, roofs and the stepped ziggurat far behind; the wide river water fills the lower part.

Babylon c. 575 BCE (after Koldewey's excavations): (1) a river quay wall of baked brick set in bitumen, 4 m high, a stair of brick going down into the water; (2) the river edge with a few reeds and a mooring post, 1 m high.
The wide brown-green Euphrates, calm water with long rows of small ripples and a slow current
The wide brown-green Euphrates, calm water with long rows of small ripples and a slow current

Babylon c. 575 BCE (after Koldewey's excavations): the skyline of Babylon from a street: dense flat-roofed houses of mudbrick and baked brick, some with toothed parapets, palm crowns between them, and far off the great stepped ziggurat and the blue towers of the Ishtar Gate.

Babylon c. 575 BCE (after Koldewey's excavations): (1) a street frontage of Babylonian houses, 7 m high: thick walls of mudbrick with vertical saw-tooth recesses, no street windows, deep plain doorways, flat roofs; (2) a low baked-brick bench along a wall, 0.5 m high.
A wide street of Babylon: packed earth with a band of baked-brick paving along the middle, dusty, a few sherds and straw
